verses.text: In the ninth year of Zedekiah's rule, on the tenth day of the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon marched against Jerusalem with his whole army. They camped around the city and built siege walls all around it.
The city was kept under siege until the eleventh year of King Zedekiah.
By the ninth day of the fourth month, the famine in the city was so bad that the people had no food left.

Then the city wall was broken through. All the soldiers ran away at night through the gate between the two walls, near the king's garden, even though the Babylonians were all around the city. The king ran toward the Jordan Valley.
But the Babylonian army chased King Zedekiah and caught up with him on the plains of Jericho. All his soldiers left him and scattered.
The Babylonians captured the king and took him to the king of Babylon at Riblah, where sentence was passed on him.
They killed Zedekiah's sons while he watched. Then they put out Zedekiah's eyes, bound him with bronze chains, and took him to Babylon.

On the seventh day of the fifth month, in the nineteenth year that Nebuchadnezzar was king of Babylon, Nebuzaradan came to Jerusalem. He was the commander of the guard and an official of the king of Babylon.
He set fire to the LORD's temple, the palace, and all the houses of Jerusalem. He burned down every important building.
The whole Babylonian army under the commander of the guard tore down the walls around Jerusalem.
Nebuzaradan, the commander of the guard, took away as prisoners the rest of the people left in the city, along with those who had gone over to the king of Babylon, and the rest of the crowd.
But the commander of the guard left behind some of the poorest people of the land to work in the vineyards and fields.
The Babylonians broke up the bronze pillars, the bronze stands, and the huge bronze tank called the Sea, which were at the LORD's temple, and they carried the bronze to Babylon.
They also took away the pots, shovels, wick trimmers, spoons, and all the bronze objects used in the temple service.
The commander of the guard took away the fire pans and the sprinkling bowls, everything made of pure gold or pure silver.
The bronze from the two pillars, the Sea, and the stands that Solomon had made for the LORD's temple was too heavy to weigh.

Each pillar was about eight metres high. The bronze top on each pillar was about one and a half metres high and was decorated all around with a network of bronze pomegranates. The second pillar, with its network, was just like the first.
The commander of the guard took as prisoners Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the priest next in rank, and the three doorkeepers.

From the people still in the city, he took the officer in charge of the soldiers, five of the king's advisers, the secretary of the army commander who called up the people of the land for war, and sixty of the people of the land who were found in the city.
Nebuzaradan, the commander of the guard, took them all and brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah.
There at Riblah, in the land of Hamath, the king of Babylon had them put to death. So the people of Judah were taken away as prisoners from their land.
Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon appointed Gedaliah son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, to be governor over the people he had left behind in Judah.

All the army officers and their men heard that the king of Babylon had made Gedaliah governor. So they came to Gedaliah at Mizpah. They were Ishmael son of Nethaniah, Johanan son of Kareah, Seraiah son of Tanhumeth from Netophah, and Jaazaniah son of the Maacathite, along with their men.
Gedaliah made a promise to them and their men. He said, "Do not be afraid of the Babylonian officials. Settle down in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and things will go well for you."

But in the seventh month, Ishmael son of Nethaniah, the son of Elishama, who was from the royal family, came with ten men. They attacked Gedaliah and killed him, along with the people of Judah and the Babylonians who were with him at Mizpah.
Then all the people, from the least to the greatest, along with the army officers, ran away to Egypt, because they were afraid of the Babylonians.

In the thirty-seventh year after Jehoiachin king of Judah was taken prisoner, on the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month, Evil-Merodach became king of Babylon. In that same year he set Jehoiachin king of Judah free from prison.
He spoke kindly to him and gave him a seat of honour higher than the other kings who were with him in Babylon.
So Jehoiachin took off his prison clothes. For the rest of his life he ate regularly at the king's table.
Every day the king gave him an allowance, for as long as he lived.
